page_title: Learn more programming languages, even if you won't use them

sources.entry: Learn more programming languages, even if you won't use them, Thorsten Ball

summary.title: Learn more programming languages, even if you won't use them
summary.one_liner: Learning new programming languages gives you different mental models and perspectives on problems, even if you never use them professionally.
takeaways: Different languages are suited to different problems, so knowing more of them lets you pick the best tool.
Each language embeds a distinct mental model for thinking about computation and program structure.
Learning a language can change how you see problems even if you never use it again, e.g. data as lists in Lisp, or memory management from C.
The author notes the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (linguistic relativity) is scientifically debated, so the mental-model claim is a personal view.
summary.summary: This short opinion essay by Thorsten Ball argues that learning new programming languages is valuable beyond practical tool selection. It uses hypothetical scenarios (string processing, concurrent financial calculations, UI work) to show that languages suit different tasks. The core argument is that each language offers a different lens or mental model, and that these perspectives persist even if you stop using the language. Examples include SQL's data flow, functional composition in Lisp, C's memory management, and React's component thinking. The author adds a footnote that the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis it draws on remains contested.
